# Summary

The author discovered two operational gotchas with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore's long-term memory system: a non-existent API method that passed code review, and a critical read-after-write consistency gap where records are immediately addressable by ID but take 15-30 seconds to appear in namespace searches. The post provides practical guidance on verifying SDK operations at build time, understanding the distinction between direct writes and semantic indexing, and implementing proper readiness checks rather than fixed delays.

# Summary

This post describes a critical blind spot in monitoring AI agents: a system can appear completely healthy while silently running expensive loops that never terminate. The author details five specific conditions that cause agents to loop indefinitely (context bloat, unsatisfiable goals, model regeneration, broken tools, and external re-drives) and explains that fixing this requires both hard technical bounds on iterations and proper instrumentation—specifically, per-session metrics that catch individual runaway sessions and fleet-wide metrics that detect gradual cost increases.

This post explains how to architect an AI agent system handling sensitive data by treating the language model as fundamentally untrustworthy and building deterministic security controls outside the model itself. The author argues that no single control is flawless, so the solution is defense-in-depth: a ranked stack of layers (identity checks, ACL filtering, tool allow-listing, query validation, and content safety) where each layer has known failure modes but no single failure exposes the data. The core principle is that the model proposes actions but never executes them—deterministic code in the system always disposes.

# Summary

The standard LLM security diagram—showing prompt injection, retrieval poisoning, context poisoning, and output injection as four separate threats—correctly identifies real attacks but misdirects defenses toward probabilistic classifiers at each stage, which an adversary can evade by scoring just below every threshold. The actual security boundary should be deterministic and deterministic code that controls what actions the system can take (tools, database queries, destinations), keyed off verified principals, rather than trying to filter attacks at the input, retrieval, context, and output layers where the attacker has influence.

# Summary

This post introduces a gap in current AI agent capabilities for incident response: while agents can read logs and call APIs, they cannot correlate real-time telemetry with organizational decisions documented in ADRs, runbooks, and planning docs. The author describes an end-to-end architecture using AWS DevOps Agent with a custom MCP server to surface both "what IS" (system state from logs/metrics) and "what SHOULD BE" (organizational intent from a curated knowledge base), demonstrating how this enables faster incident triage by connecting current symptoms to past decisions that may have expired or been deferred.

# Summary

This post explains why the author chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore over Lambda for building a production AI agent on AWS, detailing how Lambda's limitations (15-minute timeout, stateless design, session management complexity, VPC cold starts) make it unsuitable for conversational AI with persistent memory. AgentCore is presented as a managed container orchestration service purpose-built for long-running, stateful agent sessions that handles session routing, memory persistence, and streaming responses—though it trades Lambda's pay-per-invocation model for always-on container costs and has less mature tooling. The post introduces a multi-part series documenting the full production architecture from infrastructure through cost optimization.

# Summary

This post explains how the author built an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server to give a DevOps agent access to organizational decisions and documentation, rather than just infrastructure telemetry. The server exposes four tools that query a Bedrock Knowledge Base containing ADRs, runbooks, and incident reports, using structured frontmatter as a contract to enable deterministic filtering and date-based status checks. The key insight is that MCP provides a typed query layer over documented intent, solving problems with the initial approach of stuffing all documents into the system prompt—namely cost, freshness, filtering, and hallucination.

# Summary

This post documents nine specific pitfalls when deploying AWS AgentCore using CDK, including naming restrictions (no hyphens), ECR repository timing issues, missing CDK constructs requiring raw CloudFormation, VPC endpoint conflicts, KMS key policies for CloudWatch, security group egress rule handling, required parameters for runtime updates, Memory resource rollback failures, and assertion testing quirks. The author provides code examples and recovery procedures for each gotcha encountered during AgentCore CDK deployments.

# Summary

This post walks through integrating an MCP Lambda with AWS DevOps Agent using CDK, focusing on the IAM configuration and deployment architecture. The author explains a three-stack deployment pattern (KnowledgeBase → MCP Lambda → DevOps Agent), highlights key configuration choices like ARM architecture and memory sizing, and details three specific IAM gotchas encountered during implementation, including a production OIDC failure in their own pipeline.

# Summary

This post details building a Python agent application that runs inside the CDK infrastructure, using the Strands Agents SDK to power a Bedrock-backed reasoning loop with tool integration, AgentCore Memory for persistent context, and Bedrock Guardrails. The author explains why Strands was chosen over LangChain (AWS-native integration, simpler tool definitions, active development alignment), demonstrates a dual-model strategy using Claude Sonnet 4.5 for primary conversations and Amazon Nova Pro for background tasks, and highlights prompt caching as a key optimization that achieves 90% savings on cached tokens by reusing system prompts across requests.

# Summary

This post explains how to locally test a Docker-based agent before deploying to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, emphasizing the critical requirement to build images with `--platform linux/amd64` since AgentCore only runs on x86_64 architecture. The guide covers setting up a Dockerfile, configuring environment variables locally, running the container with AWS credentials, and testing the health check and invoke endpoint via curl.

# Summary

The author walks through OIDC configuration, a dual-tag ECR strategy for practical rollbacks, and multi-environment promotion with approval gates, showing an end-to-end deployment flow that takes 8-10 minutes from code push to live.

# Summary

This post covers cost optimization strategies for production AgentCore deployments, emphasizing that Bedrock model invocations are the dominant cost driver. The author details how prompt caching can save ~$480/month by charging 10x less for cached tokens, recommends using cheaper models like Amazon Nova Pro for simple tasks instead of Claude Sonnet 4.5 for everything, and provides CloudWatch alarms to catch runaway costs before they appear on your bill. For a moderately used customer service agent, the estimated monthly cost is $150-240 with these optimizations in place.

# Summary

This post explains how to enable prompt caching in AWS Bedrock's `BedrockModel` to reduce costs, which is disabled by default despite being available through two simple kwargs. The author documents a per-model compatibility issue where Amazon Nova rejects tool caching while Anthropic models accept it, provides a fast verification method using inline `usage` blocks instead of CloudWatch, and reports measured hit ratios of 99.9% on Nova and 99.8% on Sonnet resulting in 55-78% billing reductions on system-prefix tokens.

# Summary

This post documents three production lessons from diagnosing an AWS Bedrock AI workload. The author discovered that load tests can mask throttling exceptions invisible to standard metrics, that latency problems often stem from routing delays rather than model speed (measurable via TimeToFirstToken), and that prompt caching is rarely enabled despite being a simple configuration that dramatically reduces costs. The combined fixes achieved 96% cost reduction and 88% p95 latency improvement.

# Summary

The author built an AI tutoring system for his son using Claude projects and Cowork, iterating through three versions before settling on an architecture that inverts data flow—having tutoring sessions push summaries to Gmail rather than having aggregation routines pull from project chats. He identifies five production-applicable lessons: verify integration primitives before designing around them, use push architectures over pull when systems don't expose state cleanly, treat human-in-the-loop as a feature, run calibration windows before go-live, and maintain decision logs documenting what didn't work.

The author provides practical solutions including CI checks for valid SDK operations, understanding the namespace-based actor isolation model, and using polling rather than fixed sleeps for read verification.

The author describes an architecture using AWS DevOps Agent with a custom MCP server to surface both "what IS" (telemetry) and "what SHOULD BE" (organizational intent) during incidents, demonstrated through a scenario where a missed deadline on a temporary Bedrock integration becomes invisible to on-call responders until an agent correlates the incident with the expired ADR commitment.

# Summary

This post explains why the author chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore over Lambda for building a production AI agent on AWS, detailing how Lambda's stateless design, 15-minute timeout, and lack of built-in session management make it poorly suited for conversational AI workloads. AgentCore is presented as a managed container orchestration service that handles session routing, memory persistence, and long-running agent interactions, though it comes with trade-offs including idle costs and newer tooling maturity. # Summary

# Summary

This post argues that the standard "four-box" LLM security diagram (prompt injection, retrieval poisoning, context poisoning, output injection) misleads teams into building probabilistic defenses at the wrong layers. Instead, security should rely on a deterministic boundary—enumerated allowed actions, verified principals, and pre-filtered data—that the attacker cannot reach, treating classifiers as backstops rather than load-bearing controls. The author shows how this reframe prevents the endless arms race of naming new attacks and patching new vulnerabilities.
